rows.trigger: ANY grand theft (no separate dollar threshold beyond whatever made it grand theft) where the offender uses a motor vehicle as an instrumentality, other than merely as a getaway vehicle, and thereby damages the real property of another. rows.trigger: ANY grand theft where the offender causes damage to the real or personal property of another in excess of $1,000. The $1,000 figure measures DAMAGE CAUSED to a third party's property, NOT the value of the property stolen, so it is carried here in trigger only and min is null: the value stolen has NO lower bound beyond whatever made the offense grand theft, which includes value-free named items (a stolen firearm worth $200 plus $5,000 of collateral damage qualifies). 'In excess of' is strictly greater than $1,000, so exactly $1,000 of damage does not qualify.
rows.quote: 3. If the offender commits any grand theft and: ... b. In the course of committing the offense the offender causes damage to the real or personal property of another in excess of $1,000,the offender commits grand theft in the first degree, punishable as a felony of the first degree, as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

(b)1. If the property stolen is valued at $20,000 or more, but less than $100,000; ... the offender commits grand theft in the second degree, punishable as a felony of the second degree, as provided in s. 775.082, s. 775.083, or s. 775.084.

rows.quote: 2. 212.15.notes:
Fresh full walk, not a spot-check. Fetched https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/212.15 via curl and read the entire section: (1) due/delinquent dates, (2) intro + (a)-(d) + flush aggregation sentence, (3) limitations, (4) warrants/liens/garnishment.

Independent provision list vs table: the only graded offenses in the section are the six the table already carries -- (2)(a) first conviction, (2)(a) second conviction, (2)(a) third-or-subsequent conviction, (2)(b), (2)(c), (2)(d). Subsections (1), (3), and (4) assign no offense or degree ((3) is a limitations period, (4) is civil collection machinery), so they are correctly absent as rows. Nothing missing.

Degrees: all six match the statute verbatim and map onto the allowed vocabulary (second degree misdemeanor / first degree misdemeanor / third degree felony / third degree felony / second degree felony / first degree felony).

Levels independently verified against F.S. 921.0022 (2025), not assumed. A regex sweep of the whole ranking chart returns exactly one 212.15 entry: "212.15(2)(b) 3rd Failure to remit sales taxes, amount $1,000 or more but less than $20,000" under LEVEL 1 in 921.0022(3)(a). So level 1 on the (2)(b) row is correct and verifiable, and null on (2)(a) x3, (2)(c), and (2)(d) is correct -- those are unlisted offenses ranked by default under 921.0023, not guessable levels. No invented levels.

Thresholds: no false floors and no invented ceilings. min is null on all three (2)(a) rows because "less than $1,000" states no lower bound; max 1000 is a genuine exclusive trigger ceiling from the statute's own words, not a penalty cap. max is null on (2)(d) because "$100,000 or more" states no upper bound -- correctly left open rather than inferred from the tier below. (2)(b) 1000/20000 and (2)(c) 20000/100000 match "or more, but less than" exactly. All floors are inclusive ("or more"), so the absence of minExclusive is right; nothing in this section uses an "in excess of" strict threshold.

Scope: "prior" on the second-conviction and third-or-subsequent-conviction rows is the correct literal use -- those tiers turn on prior convictions, not on amount. Null elsewhere. No misuse.

Quotes: all six spot-checked character-for-character against the fetched text (more than the five required). All verbatim, including internal punctuation such as the comma before "but less than" in (b) and (c). No elisions used, none needed.

max 1000 on the two recidivist (2)(a) rows deserves a word since it could look like an inferred ceiling: it is not. Those sentences sit inside paragraph (2)(a), whose operative condition is "the total amount of stolen revenue is less than $1,000," so the recidivist tiers inherit that trigger ceiling from their own paragraph. Carrying it forward is accurate rather than invented.

unread/readWhole honesty: the section is short and fully retrievable in one fetch; I have every paragraph in hand. "unread": [] and "readWhole": true are truthful.

Cosmetic only, no penalty data affected, hence PASS not FAIL: the flush sentence "The amount of stolen revenue may be aggregated in determining the grade of the offense" is recorded only in the (2)(d) row's trigger note. Structurally it follows (d) but applies to all of subsection (2), so it also bears on the (a), (b), and (c) tiers. Any consuming page that reads triggers per-row would see it attached to the top tier alone. Worth relocating to a section-level note in a future pass, but it changes no min, max, degree, level, or scope value.

Also noted for the record: the 2025 title string in the table matches the site catchline exactly ("Taxes declared state funds; penalties for failure to remit taxes; due and delinquent dates; judicial review"), and the dollar tiers reflect the 2021-31 amendment rather than the pre-2021 $300 figure, so the table is on the current text.

fs-812.014.notes:
FULL FRESH WALK, not a spot-check. Fetched https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2025/812.014 with curl and stripped tags; built an independent provision list of 36 penalty-bearing items before opening the JSON. Also fetched s. 921.0022 with curl to test the level nulls.

COVERAGE: 42 rows. Every penalty-bearing provision I derived is present: (2)(a)1 split correctly into its value branch and its value-free semitrailer branch; (2)(a)2; (2)(a)3.a and 3.b as separate rows; (2)(b)1-4; the (2)(b) riot/emergency flush; (2)(c)1-13 all thirteen; the (2)(c) riot/emergency flush; (2)(d)1-3; (2)(e)1-3; (2)(f); (2)(g); (3)(a)-(c); (5)(b) plus 1. and 2.; (6). Non-penalty text -- (1), (3)(d), (4), (7), History -- is correctly excluded and disclosed. Nothing missing.

DEGREES: all 42 checked against the operative words. Every one matches, including the two that invert the usual ladder: (2)(d)3 (>20 dwellings) is second degree, and (2)(e)2/(e)3 turn a first degree misdemeanor into a third degree felony. (2)(b) flush = first degree felony; (2)(c) flush = second degree felony. No wrong degrees.

FALSE FLOORS: none. The four provisions most likely to attract an invented floor are all null: (2)(b)2 (cargo under $50,000, any value), (2)(d)3 (count of dwellings, not dollars), (2)(c)9 (2,000 pieces of citrus, a count), and (3)(a) (residual). Each carries the count/quantity figure in trigger text rather than in min, which is the right reading of "null where value is not the trigger."

INVENTED CEILINGS: none. (2)(a)1, (2)(a)2, (2)(b)3, (2)(b)4, (2)(d)2 and (6) all correctly carry max null where the statute states no upper bound. The $40 ceiling on (2)(e)2 and (2)(e)3 is NOT invented -- it is an element incorporated from subparagraph 1., and s. 921.0022 independently describes both offenses as "less than $40 taken from dwelling or its unenclosed curtilage," which confirms it.

INCLUSIVE/EXCLUSIVE: every max is a "less than" figure and every min is an "or more" figure, matching the stated convention. The only "in excess of" value threshold, (6)'s $3,000, is the only row carrying minExclusive true. Correct.

LEVELS: all null, with the unread field stating plainly that 921.0022 was not fetched and that no level was guessed.
